sentences.1: The farm foreman kept notes on his evening rounds.
sentences.2: He wrote that the shepherd had concluded the flock must be in the top field, since the gate stood open, and the shepherd always left that gate open only once the flock had been driven through it.
sentences.3: The foreman added, from what he saw himself, that the lower field was empty of grass.
sentences.4: The note ended with the time the rounds had finished.

bin.reason: A time of day; the language holds no 'when' beyond a stage named in a fact, so the timing word goes here.

Attribution of a conclusion to the shepherd; who concludes what is outside the language. It scopes the conclusion content and its reason to shepherd_world. The writing itself is kept as line wrote_note.
Modal of necessity; 'may, must, should, can' are outside the language.
Attribution of where the foreman's knowledge came from; who sees or knows what is outside the language. The content is what the note says and is kept in note_world.
A clock time is a number and a 'when', outside the language. The text gives no value; line note_end keeps only that the note's end carried the rounds' finish time.

readings_chosen: Sentence 1: 'kept notes' (plural) and 'the note' (sentence 4) — readings: one record kept over the rounds, or several records; chosen: one record, named note, with the singular in sentence 4 read as the same record.

Sentence 1: 'on his evening rounds' — readings: a pure occasion-and-time phrase all of it outside the language, or also a link between the keeping and the rounds that the language can hold as a fact; chosen: the link, kept as line on_rounds (said), with only 'evening' binned as a time of day.

Sentence 2: 'He wrote that ...' — readings: the writing is only the note's frame and is binned as an attribution, or the writing is a doing the narrator asserts; chosen: the doing, kept as line wrote_note, marked filled in because the sentence names no object of writing and the note is the translator's pick.

Sentence 2: 'the shepherd had concluded' — readings: the conclusion is the note's content as a whole (note_world), or the conclusion is the shepherd's and goes to his own world; chosen: the shepherd's own world, per the rule on attributed conclusions; lines flock_top, gate_stood_open, gate_rule and since1 are TOLD in shepherd_world.

Sentence 2: 'must be in the top field' — readings: 'must' is a modal of necessity and is dropped, or 'must' marks the conclusion as forced by the reason and is kept; chosen: dropped, binned as a modal; flock_top is the plain fact 'the flock is in the top field' and the force of the reason is what since1 records.

Sentence 2: 'that gate' — readings: the top field's gate, so that driving the flock through it would put the flock in the top field, or a gate whose field the text never names; chosen: the second — no line says which field the gate belongs to and no line runs from 'driven through the gate' to 'in the top field', since an added line may not let the opposite follow just as well.

Sentence 2: 'the shepherd always left that gate open only once the flock had been driven through it' — readings: one direction (his leaving the gate open never happens except after the flock has been driven through), or two directions (also, whenever he drove the flock through, he left the gate open); chosen: one direction, written as gate_rule in the direction the shepherd uses.

Sentence 2: the general line's kind — readings: MAKES or SHOWS; chosen: SHOWS, because the flock's being driven through comes before the shepherd's leaving the gate open, so the leaving cannot produce it and can only be how one tells. The word 'always' settles ALWAYS and the sentence's order settles the kind, so gate_rule adds no translator's choice.

Sentence 2: 'left that gate open' — readings: caused or allowed the gate to remain open, or departed leaving the gate open behind him; chosen: the first, the ordinary sense; both readings still leave the gate open in the shepherd's hands as the one who left it.

Sentence 2: 'since the gate stood open, and the shepherd always left that gate open only once ...' — readings: two reasons each offered on its own, or one reason (the gate's standing open) with the second clause as the rule that licenses the step; chosen: the second — since1 is one SINCE line pointing at gate_stood_open, with gate_rule kept in the ledger as the rule the checker can use by any route.

Sentence 2: the gap between 'the gate stood open' (gate_stood_open) and 'the shepherd leaves the gate open' (gate_rule's condition) — readings: they are the same for the ledger (the gate stands open as he left it), or they are different and the link is unstated; chosen: the second — no line links them, so the checker can report the step as unstated.

Sentence 3: 'from what he saw himself' — readings: it makes the content a claim about the actual world on the foreman's own authority, or it is an attribution of where the foreman's knowledge came from; chosen: the attribution, binned as who-knows-what, with the content kept as what the note says (TOLD in note_world).

Sentence 3: 'added' — readings: the object of adding is the statement, which the translator would have to name, or the doing can be written with the note as what he added to; chosen: the second — added_note is 'foreman ADDED TO note', marked filled in because the sentence names no object.

Sentence 4: 'the note ended with the time the rounds had finished' — readings: the whole phrase is the note's content (TOLD in note_world), or the narrator's own description of the note's last entry with 'the rounds had finished' as a relative clause he takes for granted; chosen: the second — note_end is CLAIMED, rounds_done is GIVEN, and the clock value 'the time' is binned.

Sentences 1 to 3: the verbs 'kept', 'wrote' and 'added' have no shape in the shape book — readings: substitute a shaped verb, or write the text's own verb and let the checker report 'not checked'; chosen: the text's own verb in each happening.
Spelling: no slips of spelling in the text; nothing open, nothing taken.
